projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Norbert Woolley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: MAY 15, 2002 WITH NORBERT WILLIS WOOLLEY, W-O-O-L-L-E-Y. DATE OF BIRTH 10-21-1925. MR. WOOLLEY RESIDES AT 2313 EAST CHANNEL AVENUE IN EVANSVILLE, INDIANA. A NATIVE OF TABUNDO (PH), INDIANA AREA. SERVED IN THE UNITED STATES NAVY IN WORLD WAR II AND ALSO IN KOREA. HE SERVED IN KOREA FROM JANUARY 19 -- EXCUSE ME -- IN WORLD WAR II FROM JANUARY 1944 TO MARCH 1946. FOLLOWING WORLD WAR II HE JOINED THE RESERVES AND WAS CALLED BACK TO ACTIVE DUTY IN THE KOREAN CONFLICT AND SERVED FROM 1950 UNTIL 1952.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: MR. WOOLLEY, PLEASE TELL ME -- I'LL BEGIN THE TAPE -- HOW DOES IT HAPPEN -- WHERE WERE YOU BOTH LIVING AT THE TIME WHEN YOU RECEIVED YOUR DRAFT NOTICE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OKAY. I WAS LIVING IN EVANSVILLE, INDIANA, AND I WAS WORKING AT A PLACE CALLED HERMAN DAIRY, AND I ENTERED -- WAS GIVEN A CHOICE OF THE NAVY, AIR CORP OR ARMY. I CHOSE THE NAVY BECAUSE I HAD TWO BROTHERS FIGHTING IN WORLD WAR II IN THE ARMY, AND I LEFT EVANSVILLE IN -- WE HAD BOOT CAMP IN GREAT LAKES, ILLINOIS. I ORGINALLY WAS IN COMPANY 266, BUT I TRIED OUT FOR CHOIR COMPANY, AND THAT TOOK A WEEK FOR THEM TO GET 130 GUYS THAT THEY FELT COULD SING. SO I ENDED UP IN COMPANY 277 IN GREAT LAKES. AND WE REHEARSED TWO HOURS A DAY, SANG FOR A MEET YOUR NAVY PROGRAM ON FRIDAY NIGHTS AND TWO CHURCH SERVICES ON SUNDAY. AND I WENT NINE WEEKS TO BOOT CAMP.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: TELL ME ABOUT BOOT CAMP. THAT WAS ALSO --

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: THAT WAS IN GREAT LAKES.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHAT WAS THE DAILY ROUTINE LIKE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: DAILY ROUTINE, WELL, WE HAD TO GET UP AND SHOWER, AND THEN YOU HAD TO MAKE SURE THAT YOU COULD BOUNCE A QUARTER OFF YOUR BED BECAUSE YOU HAD AN INSPECTION, YOU HAD BARRACKS INSPECTION. AND YOUR DAY CONSISTED OF MARCHING, LEARNING VARIOUS THINGS, AND THEN WE HAD CHOIR REHEARSAL TWO HOURS EVERY DAY. AND WE HAD TO SING EVERY FRIDAY AND TWO HOURS ON SUNDAY, BUT WE WENT NINE WEEKS. WE HAD A BARRACKS INSPECTION EVERY DAY. YOUR BUNK WAS INSPECTED EVERY DAY. AND IF YOU COULDN'T BOUNCE A QUARTER OFF THE BED, THEN YOU GOT DEMERITS, AND YOU HAD A FEW CHALLENGES TO FACE. BUT WE WERE FORTUNATE, WE WON THE BARRACKS INSPECTION FLAG EVERY WEEK. AND YOU HAVE A MARCHING CONTEST THE LAST TWO WEEKS AND OUR GROUP WON THE MARCHING FLAG AT THE END. AND I THINK PEOPLE NEED TO REMEMBER WE WERE A CHOIR COMPANY, AND WE HAD GOOD RHYTHM.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WELL, TELL ME ABOUT THE CHOIR COMPANY. I WASN'T EVEN SURE THAT THAT EXISTED. TELL ME ABOUT THAT.

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WELL, THEY TOOK A WEEK TO TRY PEOPLE OUT.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: DID YOU HAVE A REAL INTEREST IN DOING THAT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OH, I LOVE TO SING. I WAS IN THE HIGH SCHOOL CHOIR, AND I ENDED UP SINGING WITH 130 GUYS. WE REHEARSED TWICE A DAY. WE WOULD SING IN FOUR PARTS. AND I REALLY LIKED GOING TO MEET YOUR NAVY ON FRIDAY NIGHT BECAUSE YOU GOT TO GO TO THE MARINE BASE. AND ONE OF THE HIGHLIGHTS IS THEY HAD A YOUNG STARLETT BACK THEN THAT THEY BROUGHT ON THIS MEET YOUR NAVY PROGRAM, AND I GOT TO SIT NEXT TO HER, AND HER NAME WAS SUSAN HAYWORTH, GOOD LOOKING GAL. AND SO THEN AFTER NINE WEEKS I FINISHED MY BOOT CAMP, WAS GIVEN A LEAVE. I CAME HOME TO EVANSVILLE, AND THEN MY ORDERS SENT ME TO A PLACE CALLED THE DISTRIBUTION CENTER CALLED SHOEMAKER, CALIFORNI

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHEN YOU GOT ON THE TRAIN, DID THEY TELL WHAT YOUR THE DESTINATION WAS?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES. I HAD MY ORDERS. I KNEW I WAS GOING TO SHOEMAKER, CALIFORNIA, BUT I DIDN'T THINK IT SHOULD TAKE ME DAYS TO GET TO CALIFORNIA. BUT THEY DERAILED OUR TRAIN EVERY TIME A FREIGHT TRAIN OR SOMETHING CAME BY. BUT IT WAS AN INTERESTING TRIP.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: ROUGHLY HOW MANY MEN MIGHT HAVE BEEN ON THAT TRAIN?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: I'D SAY 300.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WAS IT KIND OF CRAMPED QUARTERS?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES. IT WAS PRETTY CRAMPED. BUT WE WERE ALL GOING TO THE SAME PLACE. WE WERE ALL GOING TO SHOEMAKER, CALIFORNIA, WHICH WAS A RECEIVING DISTRIBUTION CENTER. IT WAS ABOUT 15 MILES FROM OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA, THE MIDDLE OF NOWHERE, AND STAYED THERE ABOUT A WEEK AND A HALF, AND THEN I WAS PLACED ON AN LST TO GO TO HAWAII TO ANOTHER RECEIVING STATION. AND WHEN I GOT TO HAWAII, I WAS THERE ABOUT A WEEK, AND THEN I WAS SENT ON THE USS VINSON, WHICH WAS A LIGHT CRUISER TO A PLACE CALLED ENEWETAK IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PACIFIC, AND IN ENEWETAK I PICKED UP MY SHIP, THE USS WASP CV-18. AND WHEN I GOT ON THE SHIP, I ASKED THEM WHICH DIVISION DOESN'T HAVE KP. AND THEY TOLD ME K DIVISION AND I TOLD THEM THAT WAS THE DIVISION THAT I WANTED TO BE IN.

SO I WAS ASSIGNED TO K DIVISION AND I BECAME A COMMUNICATION YEOMAN. AND MY JOB STARTED OUT AS WHAT THEY CALL A STRIKER. MY JOB WAS TO RUN MESSAGES ALL OVER THE USS WASP TO PEOPLE LIKE THE EXECUTIVE OFFICER, THE FLIGHT OFFICER, THE CAPTAIN, THE GUNNERY OFFICER, AND THEN I HAD TO DO THE FILING IN THE OFFICE. AND THEN AS YOU ADVANCED, I MADE SENIOR FIRST CLASS. I BECAME WHAT YOU CALLED A SKIDS MAN. RADIO ONE, WHICH IS THREE DECKS ABOVE US, WOULD SEND DOWN MESSAGES, WE'D PASS THEM IN TO A DECODER ROOM, COMMUNICATION ROOM, WHICH WE WERE NOT PERMITTED IN, AND THE DIFFERENT OFFICERS WERE ASSIGNED, THEY'D BREAK THE CODE, THEN WE'D TYPE UP THE MESSAGES, AND IF THEY WERE CONFIDENTIAL, WE'D PUT THEM IN A METAL BOX, AND THEN THE MESSENGER, WHOEVER THAT WAS ASSIGNED TO THAT, WOULD SEE THAT THEY WERE TAKEN ALL OVER THE SHIP. AND THEN WHEN I MADE THIRD CLASS, I BECAME THE YEOMAN.

I RAN THE OFFICE. I GUESS ONE OF THE HIGHLIGHTS OF ME BEING IN THE COMMUNICATION OFFICE WAS FRANKLIN ROOSEVELT'S SON, YOUNGEST SON, JOHN, WAS THE ASSISTANT SUPPLY OFFICER ON MY SHIP, THE WASP, AND HE WAS ASSIGNED TO BREAK CODE IN THE COMMUNICATION ROOM. SO I GOT TO MEET JOHN ROOSEVELT. AND, YOU KNOW, I ALWAYS THOUGHT A PRESIDENT'S SON HAD A LOT OF CLOUT, BUT TO SHOW YOU THE PATRIOTISM OF THE ROOSEVELTS, WHEN HIS FATHER DIED, HE STAYED ABOARD SHIP. HE DID NOT GO HOME FOR THE FUNERAL, NOR DID HIS BROTHER WHO WAS THE COMMANDER OF THE DESTROYER FRANKLIN, AND HE STAYED IN COMMAND OF HIS DESTROYER. NEITHER ONE OF THEM GOT TO GO HOME FOR THEIR FATHER'S FUNERAL. BUT I SERVED ON THE WASP UNTIL THE END OF THE WAR.

AS I SAID, I WAS A COMMUNICATION YEOMAN. WE FOUGHT IN A LOT OF BATTLES STARTING WITH WAKE ISLAND. PROBABLY ONE OF THE GREATEST EXPERIENCES THAT I EVER REMEMBER WAS WHEN WE WERE FIGHTING IN THE BATTLE OF THE MARIANA ISLANDS, WHICH WAS SAIPAN, GUAM, TINIAN, THAT GROUP OF ISLANDS, WE WERE HUNTING THE JAP FLEET. WE WERE A TASK FORCE 58, AND ADMIRABLE MITSCHER WAS THE COMMANDER OF THAT TASK FORCE, AND WE HAD SPOTTED THE FLEET SO WE WERE SEARCHING TO FIND THEM. AND WE STARTED THE SAIPAN OPERATION ON JUNE 6TH OF '44, AND FINALLY ON JUNE 20TH AT ABOUT 2130 P.M. THEY FOUND THE FLEET. AND OUR LEADERS KNEW THAT OUR PLANES DID NOT HAVE ENOUGH GAS TO ATTACK THE JAPANESE TASK AND GET BACK, BUT THEY WERE ASSIGNED TO ATTACK THEM ANYWAY.

PROBABLY ONE OF THE GREATEST EXPERIENCES THAT I REMEMBER IS WHEN THE PLANES CAME BACK FROM THE STRIKE AFTER THEY HAD FOUND THE FLEET AND DESTROYED A LOT OF THEIR SHIPS, THEY TURNED ON ALL THE SPOTLIGHTS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PACIFIC OCEAN -- AND NORMALLY YOU DON'T LAND PLANES THAT DON'T BELONG TO YOUR SHIP BUT ADMIRAL MITSCHER PUT OUT THE MESSAGE THAT YOU LAND ANYBODY THAT CAN GET -- CAN FIND YOUR SHIP, AND I STOOD ON THE FLIGHT DECK WATCHING PLANES CIRCLE OUR SHIP. AND THEY WOULD -- I COULD HEAR THE RADIO AND THEY'D SAY THEY ARE RUNNING OUT OF GAS, AND YOU COULD ACTUALLY SEE THEM HITTING THE WATER IN THE OCEAN BECAUSE THEY RAN OUT OF GAS. BUT THAT NIGHT OUR SHIP LANDED ANYBODY.

THEY DIDN'T CARE WHAT SHIP IT WAS FROM. THEY DIDN'T CARE IF IT WAS FROM THE HORNET. THEY DIDN'T CARE IF IT FROM THE FRANKLIN, WHATEVER. THEY CAME DOWN, WE LANDED IT. BUT THAT WAS A TREMENDOUS EXPERIENCE FOR ME TO SEE ALL THOSE SPOTLIGHTS LIGHTING UP THE MIDDLE BECAUSE, YOU KNOW, YOU WERE UNDER CONDITION BLACK ALL THE TIME, HAD YOUR HATCHES ALL, YOU KNOW, DARK ON ACCOUNT OF SUBMARINES.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: DO YOU HAVE ANY IDEA WHAT THE LOSSES WERE MAYBE FOR THE U.S. IN THAT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WE PROBABLY LOST I WOULD SAY A HUNDRED PLANES, AND WE PROBABLY LOST 35 TO 50 MEN. WE SPENT THE NEXT THREE DAYS LOOKING FOR PILOTS AND CREWMEN. WE DIDN'T -- AFTER WE HAD ATTACHED TO THE FLEET, WE JUST SPENT THE NEXT THREE DAYS LOOKING FOR SURVIVORS.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: DID YOU HAVE SOME RESCUES?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES, WE DID. WE --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: TELL ME ABOUT SOME OF THOSE.

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WE FOUND PEOPLE. WHAT YOU DO IS A DESTROYER WOULD COME UP, AND THEY'D PICK THEM UP, AND THEN THEY'D BRING THEM OVER TO THE CHAIRS, AND THEY BROUGHT THEM OUT IN CHAIRS AND IN A BASKET, YOU'D HOOK UP TO A RIG, AND THEY'D TRANSFER THEM FROM THE DESTROYER TO THE AIRCRAFT CARRIER. NOW AIRCRAFT CARRIERS HAD THE FACILITY TO MAKE ICE CREAM SO EVERY TIME THEY BROUGHT US BACK PILOTS, WE'D SEND THEM OVER FIVE GALLONS OF ICE CREAM. BUT IT'S AN EXPERIENCE TO WATCH PEOPLE PLUCK PEOPLE OUT OF THE OCEAN AND THEN TIE UP WITH YOU AND HAVE THEM IN A BASKET, SEND THEM BACK TO YOU SO YOU CAN GET THEM BACK TO WHERE THEY BELONG SO THEY CAN GET IN THE AIRPLANE --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: I'M SURE THAT HAD TO BE EQUALLY EMOTIONAL NOT ONLY FOR THE PEOPLE THAT WERE RESCUED BUT FOR THE MEN WHO WERE LIFTING THEM UP?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: IT WAS VERY EMOTIONAL, BUT IT MADE YOU FEEL VERY GOOD, YOU KNOW, BECAUSE IT MADE US FEEL GOOD BECAUSE WE FOUND THAT FLEET, YOU KNOW. THE ADMIRAL KNEW WHEN HE ORDERED THE FLEET TO GO AHEAD, THAT WE HAD PILOTS THAT WOULD NOT HAVE ENOUGH GAS TO GET BACK, AND THE PILOTS KNEW THAT, THE PILOTS KNEW THAT. EVERYBODY ON MY SHIP KNEW IT.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: HOW DAMAGING WAS THIS ATTACK?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: IT WAS VERY DAMAGING TO THE JAPANESE BECAUSE FROM THAT TIME ON, I WOULD SAY WE WERE THE AGGRESSORS AND THE JAPANESE WERE THE DEFENDERS FROM THAT TIME ON. WE HAD A VERY SUCCESSFUL LAUNCH, A VERY SUCCESSFUL HIT.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHAT KIND OF A RESPONSE WERE THEY ABLE TO MUSTER?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: THEY -- WELL, WHEN YOU GOT FLASHLIGHT -- SPOTLIGHTS GOING STRAIGHT UP AND YOU DON'T GET ATTACKED, I'D SAY THEY WERE MORE INTERESTED IN TRYING TO AVOID WHAT WE WERE DOING THAN TRYING TO HIT US. THAT DOESN'T MEAN LATER ON THEY DIDN'T TRY TO HIT US BECAUSE THEY DID, YOU KNOW. WE KEPT ON -- WE WERE SUCCESSFUL IN SAIPAN AND TINIAN AND GUAM. WE WON THE MARIANAS. WE WON IWO JIMA. WE WENT ON FROM THERE, YOU KNOW, AND WE RAN INTO THE CHINA SEA. THE SHIP I WAS ON, THE WASP CV-18, WE WERE IN FIVE TYPHOONS, AND WE HIT A TYPHOON WHEN -- AFTER THE WAR WAS OVER, AND KNOCKED DOWN 20 FEET OF MY FLIGHT DECK, SOLID STEEL.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT -- HOW HORRENDOUS IS IT GOING THROUGH A TYPHOON? WHAT IS THAT LIKE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WELL, IT'S SCARY. FIRST PLACE YOU BATTEN DOWN ALL THE HATCHES SO YOU DON'T GET ANY WATER INSIDE AND EVEN A SHIP AS LARGE AS AN AIRCRAFT CARRIER, YOU HAVE NO CONTROL. YOUR DANGER IS NOT FROM CAPSIZING. YOUR DANGER IS THAT OTHER SHIPS THAT ARE IN YOUR FLEET HAVE NO CONTROL AND THEY COULD RAM AGAINST YOU, YOU KNOW. EVEN MY SHIP HAD NO CONTROL BECAUSE THE AFT PART OF THE SHIP IS UP AND DOWN OUT OF THE WATER, AND YOUR RUDDERS AND THE AFT PART OF THE SHIP, AND YOU JUST HAVE NO STEERING CONTROL SO IT'S VERY DANGEROUS. AND WHEN YOU HAVE WAVES WITH TREMENDOUS FORCE, AND YOU THINK THE SIZE OF AN AIRCRAFT CARRIER, AND THESE WAVES COME UP OVER A FLIGHT DECK, AND THEN WHEN YOU THINK OUR FLIGHT DECK IS SOLID STEEL, IT BENT 20 FEET TREMENDOUSLY.

FORTUNATELY THAT WAS AFTER THE WAR WAS OVER. IT WAS NOT WHEN WE WERE IN COMBAT OR THE WAR WAS OVER, BUT IT'S -- YOU CAN'T EAT VERY WELL BECAUSE IF YOU ARE IN THE GALLEY AND THEY ARE FEEDING YOU, YOUR PLATE GOES FROM ONE SIDE TO THE OTHER. IF YOU DON'T HOLD YOUR PLATE, YOU ARE NOT GOING TO EAT. SO IT'S AN EXPERIENCE, BUT, YOU KNOW, YOU SURVIVED IT. THE MAIN CONCERN YOU HAD WHEN YOU SERVE ON ANY SHIP, I DON'T CARE IF IT'S AIRCRAFT CARRIER, DESTROYER, WHATEVER, IS YOU WANT TO KEEP THE SHIP AFLOAT.

YOU KNOW, TWO GRAVE DANGERS. ONE IS KEEPING IT AFLOAT AND THE OTHER ONE IS DON'T GET A FIRE. SO THAT'S WHEN YOU ARE ON THE SHIP. ONE OF THE CHALLENGES WE FACED, YOU KNOW -- WE FOUGHT THE BATTLE OF OKINAWA AND AT THE BATTLE OF OKINAWA MY SHIP GOT HIT. WE GOT HIT WITH A 500 POUND BOMB AND THE BOMB EXPLODED BETWEEN OUR --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: I HAVE NO IDEA HOW TO COMPREHEND HOW DECISIVE A BOMB LIKE THAT IS. IS THERE ANYTHING YOU CAN COMPARE IT TO? A 500 POUND BOMB, WHAT IS THAT LIKE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WELL, IT EXPLODED BETWEEN THE LAUNDRY WHICH IS ON THE FOURTH DECK AND THE GALLEY. THAT'S WHERE IT EXPLODED. WE WERE AT CONDITION ONE. WE HAD BEEN UNDER ATTACK FOR THREE DAYS. ALL THE RADAR SHOWED THAT NOBODY WAS UP THERE. SO WE WENT FROM GENERAL QUARTERS TO CONDITION ONE. AND CONDITION ONE IS WHEN HALF OF YOUR PEOPLE WE TRY TO FEED THEM AND THE OTHER HALF REMAIN ON THEIR GUN CREWS. AND OUR GALLEY WAS FULL AT THE TIME THAT THE BOMB EXPLODED SO WE LOST APPROXIMATELY 169 PEOPLE PLUS WE HAD AT LEAST ABOUT 300 AND SOME ODD THAT WERE WOUNDED. AND AT THAT TIME WE WERE IN COMBAT SO WHAT THEY DID IS THEY WELDED THE HOLE IN THE FLIGHT DECK SHUT SO WE COULD CONTINUE TO LAND PLANES, AND THEN WE HAD A DIVISION CALLED DIVISION ONE AND THAT'S THE REPAIR DIVISION AND SO THAT DIVISION SET ABOUT REPAIRING THE DAMAGE BELOW THE DECK WHILE WE WERE RUNNING.

OF COURSE, THE MAJOR THING IS GET THE FIRE OUT AND GET SOME STEEL AGAINST THE HOLE THAT YOU HAVE IN THE BULKHEAD AND OUR DIVISION ONE CREWS WERE SUCCESSFUL. THEY GOT IT DONE AND WE STAYED IN COMBAT. AND -- BUT IT'S DEVASTATING BECAUSE YOU HAVE TO REALIZE IF YOU GOT A FIRE BELOW DECK, YOU GOT A LOT OF SMOKE. IT'S LIKE ANY OTHER FIRE AND UNTIL YOU GET THAT FIRE OUT, YOU ARE GOING TO HAVE A LOT OF THEM THAT ARE GOING TO DIE FROM SMOKE INHALATION.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: THAT'S PROBABLY WHAT HAPPENED HERE, RIGHT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YEAH. WE HAD A LOT OF PEOPLE THAT DIED FROM SMOKE INHALATION. YOU CAN'T UNDERSTAND THE COMBUSTION OF A BOMB, AND THE REASON FOR THAT IS WE WERE FEEDING AT THE TIME AND WE HAD CHOW LINES, AND WHEN THE BOMB EXPLODED, YOU'D HAVE SOMEBODY STANDING ON THE HANGAR DECK IN A LINE, AND SOME GUY WOULD GET AN ARM BLOWN OFF AND NOTHING HAPPENED TO THE NEXT GUY. SO IT'S -- YOU DON'T KNOW HOW THE COMBUSTION IS GOING TO BLAST. IT'S -- THERE'S NO RECOLLECTION. AND FOR ME I'M FORTUNATE I -- AT THAT TIME I HAD TWO PLACES TO BE IN GENERAL QUARTERS. I EITHER HAD TO BE IN THE COMMUNICATION OFFICE OR I HAD TO BE IN WHAT THEY CALLED THE ADMIRAL'S QUARTERS.

IT WAS MY JOB WHEN I WASN'T IN THE OFFICE WAS TO IF WE HAD TO ABANDON SHIP, TAKE ALL SECRET PAPERS, PUT THEM IN A LEAD BAG AND IF WE HAD TO ABANDON SHIP, I HAD TO MAKE SURE THEY WERE DROPPED OVER AND SUNK. SO I HAPPENED TO BE IN WHAT WE CALL THE BULK WHEN THE BOMB HIT THE SHIP AND THE BULK'S BETWEEN THE FLIGHT DECK AND HANGAR DECK. SO IT DID NOT HIT IN MY AREA. AND WHEN I OPENED MY HATCH, WHEN I HEARD THE EXPLOSION, I JUST GOT A HUGE PUFF OF SMOKE.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: NORB, I HAVE A QUESTION.

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: SURE.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: IN A SITUATION LIKE THIS, IS EVERYONE TO STAY ON THE SHIP UNLESS -- DO YOU HAVE TO WAIT FOR AN ORDER TO ABANDON SHIP?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: NO.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHAT'S THE PROTOCOL?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WHEN YOU'RE GENERAL QUARTERS, EVERYBODY IS NOT ON IT YET. THE FIRST LIEUTENANT'S DIVISION IS A STATION, THE RADIO MEN ARE AT A STATION. I'M AT A STATION. IF YOU ARE NOT AT YOUR DUTY STATION, YOU HAVE AN ASSIGNED PLACE THAT YOU HAVE TO BE. AND WHILE YOU WERE AT SEA THEY HAVE DRILLS EVERY WEEK, AND I DON'T CARE WHAT HAPPENS, YOU HAVE TO CARRY OUT THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT YOU ARE GIVEN. IF YOU ARE IN THE FIRST LIEUTENANT DIVISION, YOUR JOB IS TO MAKE SURE THAT THE SHIP GETS REPAIRED, THE FIRE'S PUT OUT AND THE SHIP STAYS AFLOAT. IF YOU HAD A GUN, YOUR JOB IS TO STAY AT THAT GUN.

EVERYBODY HAS AN ASSIGNED TASK, AND THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT YOU ARE SUPPOSED TO DO. AND THAT'S WHAT EVERYBODY DOES BECAUSE THEY KNOW IF THEY DON'T CARRY OUT THEIR ORDER, THEY COULD CAUSE THE DEATH OF SOMEBODY ELSE. YOU KNOW, IT'S NOT EASY TO CLOSE THE HATCH TO SAVE THE SHIP WHEN YOU KNOW YOU GOT SOMEBODY ELSE BEHIND THE HATCH, BUT THAT HAPPENED ON MY SHIP BECAUSE THAT'S THE WAY YOU ARE TAUGHT. YOU KEEP THE SHIP SAFE, AND YOU DO WHAT YOU HAVE TO DO. WE HAD GUYS TRAPPED -- WE HAD GUYS TRAPPED IN COMPARTMENTS THAT THE ONLY WAY THEY GOT OUT WAS GO UP INTO THE CEILING WHERE THE AIR PASSAGES WERE AND CRAWL THROUGH THOSE AIR VENTS TO SAFETY BECAUSE THEY COULDN'T GET OUT OF THE COMPARTMENT THEY WERE IN.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: DID SOME OF THEM DO THAT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES. FOR SOME OF THEM GOT DROWNED, PARTICULARLY IN A COMPARTMENT WHERE THE HOLE WAS AND YOU GOT TO SHUT THAT HATCH BECAUSE YOU DON'T WANT THE REST OF IT TO FLOOD THE SHIP, BUT IN PLACES THAT DIDN'T HAVE THE WATER COMING IN, YOU HAD GUYS THAT FOUND THE AIR VENTS AND THEY FOUND A WAY TO -- YOU KNOW, PEOPLE BECOME GENIUSES WHEN IT COMES TO SURVIVAL. AND WE HAD A LOT OF GUYS TRAPPED BEHIND THE BULKHEAD THAT GOT THROUGH THE AIR VENTS AND GOT TO SAFETY, BUT THEY ARE SMART ENOUGH TO KNOW THAT.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WOULD YOU SAY THIS WAS THE SINGLE WORST INCIDENT THAT YOU EXPERIENCED OR WAS IT --

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: I WOULD SAY THE DAY WE GOT HIT AT OKINAWA WAS THE WORST THAT I HAVE. AND THE SECOND WORST WAS WE STAYED OUT INTO COMBAT FOR FIVE MORE DAYS, AND I HAD TO WALK AT NIGHT TO MY QUARTERS TO SLEEP, AND I HAD TO WALK THE FLIGHT DECK BECAUSE YOU ARE DARK, AND I HAD TO WALK THE HANGAR DECK AND I HAD TO PASS BY 169 DEAD BODIES FOR FIVE DAYS. THAT WAS THE SECOND WORST EXPERIENCE THAT I HAD, WALKING BY THOSE BECAUSE YOU DON'T FORGET THAT. WHEN WE GOT TO SAFETY, FINALLY, THEN WE HAD A BURIAL AND I WATCHED ALL 169 OF THOSE GUYS DROPPED OVER THE SIDE OF MY SHIP ONE AT A TIME WITH AN AMERICAN FLAG ON TOP OF THE CASKET.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHERE WAS THAT, NORB?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: IT WAS OUT IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PACIFIC RIGHT OFF OF OKINAWA. AND, OF COURSE, ONCE WE GOT OUT OF COMBAT WE BURIED OUR CREW AND THEN WE HEADED AGAIN TO ENEWETAK.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: THAT HAD TO BE A HORRIBLE THING TO VIEW.

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES, IT IS. IT'S REALLY HORRIBLE. YOU KNOW, WE HAD A LOT OF GUYS THAT GOT HURT THAT DIDN'T EVEN GO TO SICK BAY BECAUSE THEY KNEW WHERE OTHER PEOPLE WERE HURT SO BAD THAT THEY NEEDED THE HELP BEFORE THEY DID. WE HAD A LOT OF GUYS THAT WAITED TO GO TO SICK BAY BECAUSE THEY DIDN'T FEEL THEY WERE HURT THAT BAD. AND WE STAYED IN COMBAT AND ONCE WE GOT OUT, WE BURIED THEM, AND THEN WE WENT TO ENEWETAK WHICH IS A SUPPLY PLACE, WAITED THERE TWO DAYS AND THEY DECIDED THEY COULDN'T REPAIR US SO WE WENT BACK TO PEARL HARBOR. AFTER THAT WE WERE SENT TO BREMERTON, WASHINGTON TO GET REPAIRED. THAT TOOK TWO MONTHS. ONCE WE WERE REPAIRED, WE HEADED RIGHT BACK OUT TO THE PACIFIC.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: SO WHEN YOU CAME -- WHEN YOU CAME TO BREMERTON, THAT WAS THE FIRST TIME BACK ON --

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: THE FIRST TIME I HAD BEEN BACK TO THE STATES.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: OKAY. WHAT WAS THAT LIKE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: AND I GOT 30 DAYS LEAVE.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: I MEAN DID FAMILIES COME THERE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OH, YEAH.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: SO WHAT WAS IT LIKE, A LOT OF THE FAMILIES THAT DIDN'T HAVE ANYONE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OH, YOU HAD A LOT OF PEOPLE THAT DIDN'T HAVE ANYBODY TO COME BACK TO WHEN YOU LOSE 169 MEN, YOU KNOW. WE SAT OUT OFF THE COAST OF SEATTLE FOR TWO DAYS WHILE THEY UNLOADED ALL THE AMMUNITION OFF THE SHIP, AND THEN THE FIRST LEAVE PARTY WENT HOME AND THOSE OF US THAT WERE IN THE SECOND LEAVE PARTY GOT LIBERTY EVERY OTHER DAY. AND I WENT HOME ON LEAVE, AND THEN I CAME BACK AND THEN WE HEADED BACK OUT TO THE PACIFIC AND WE PICKED UP TASK FORCE 38 AND FINISHED THE WAR. AND WE WERE OFF THE COAST OF JAPAN SENDING FLIGHTS OUT AND WHEN THE WAR ENDED, WE WERE OFF THE COAST OF JAPAN.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: YOU WERE THERE WHEN THE BOMBS WERE DROPPED, RIGHT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES. SURE WAS.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: HOW MUCH DID -- COMMON KNOWLEDGE WAS IT THAT THE U.S. POSSESSED SOMETHING OF THAT SIZE?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: IT WASN'T A LOT OF COMMON KNOWLEDGE TO US UNTIL AFTER IT HAPPENED.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: HOW DID YOU GET THE NEWS?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OVER THE RADIO. OVER THE RADIO.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WHAT DID YOU HEAR? WHAT DO YOU REMEMBER ABOUT THAT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: I REMEMBER THEY TOLD US THEY DROPPED A BOMB, AND IT WAS AN ATOMIC BOMB, AND WE WERE RIGHT OFF OF THE COAST OF JAPAN WHEN I GOT THE NEWS.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: WERE YOU ABLE TO COMPREHEND THE SIZE OF IT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: I WASN'T AT THAT TIME, BUT THEN I -- THEN WE GOT THE MESSAGE THEY DROPPED A SECOND BOMB, AND I THINK THAT REALLY HIT HOME, AND THEN WE GOT THE MESSAGE THAT JAPAN HAD SURRENDERED.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: DID YOU FEEL MAYBE AFTER THE FIRST ONE THAT THE WAR WAS NEARING THE END?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: YES, SURE DID. AND, OF COURSE, ONCE WE HEARD THE WAR WAS OVER, WE WERE ALL ELATED. I WAS DISAPPOINTED BECAUSE I WANTED TO GO INTO JAPAN, BUT SINCE WE HAD 20 FEET OF OUR FLIGHT DECK KNOCKED DOWN, WE HAD TO COME BACK TO THE STATES.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: NO DOUBT THAT PROBABLY SAVED LOTS AND LOTS OF LIVES?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: I WOULD SAY I THINK HARRY TRUMAN MADE THE RIGHT DECISION. AND, YOU KNOW, PEOPLE TALK ABOUT HOW HORRIBLE IT WAS. I THINK THAT PEOPLE FAIL TO REALIZE THE ATROCITIES BOTH THE NAZIS AND VIETNAMESE PUT ON OUR PEOPLE IN PRISON CAMPS, AND DROPPING THE BOMB SAVED THOUSANDS AND THOUSANDS OF AMERICAN LIVES, YOU KNOW. AND PEOPLE SAY WAR IS HELL AND WAR IS HELL. THERE'S NO JOY IN A WAR. THEY MAKE MOVIES ON HOW GLORIOUS WAR IS. THERE'S NOTHING GLORIOUS ABOUT SEEING GUYS KILLED, SEEING GUYS HAVE A LEG BLOWN OFF, ARM BLOWN OFF.

THERE'S NOTHING GLORIOUS ABOUT IT. BUT WHEN YOU FIGHT, YOU FIGHT TO WIN. AND ONE OF THE THINGS I'M PROUD OF IS WE WON WORLD WAR II. I FOUGHT IN THE KOREAN WAR, AND I GUESS ONE OF THE BIGGEST UPSETS I HAD IN THE KOREAN WAR WAS WE HAD IT WON AND WE GOT STOPPED AT THE 48TH PARALLEL, WE HAD TO MOVE BACK AND THERE HASN'T BEEN A WAR SINCE WORLD WAR II THAT WE REALLY FOUGHT TO WIN. THAT UPSETS ME AS A VETERAN.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: NORB, AFTER THE WAR YOU CAME BACK TO THIS AREA, RIGHT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: AFTER THE WAR I CAME HOME, STAYED IN THE RESERVE, WENT TO WORK BACK AT HERMAN DAIRY, AND THEN I DECIDED TO GO TO COLLEGE ON THE G.I. BILL. I WENT TO THE UNIVERSITY OF EVANSVILLE AND MAJORED IN EDUCATION, WENT YEAR ROUND BECAUSE I GOT MARRIED TO A WONDERFUL WIFE WHO I'VE BEEN MARRIED TO FOR 54 YEARS, EVELYN. AND WHEN I GOT OUT OF COLLEGE, I STARTED TEACHING SCHOOL AT A SCHOOL CALLED WEST HEIGHTS. AND THE DAY I STARTED TEACHING I GOT CALLED BACK INTO THE KOREAN WAR.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: THE DAY YOU STARTED TEACHING?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: THE DAY I STARTED TEACHING SCHOOL, I GOT MY ORDERS TO GO BACK TO THE NAVY.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: HOW WAS YOUR REACTION TO THAT? WHAT WAS YOUR WIFE'S REACTION?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: MY REACTION WAS OKAY. YOU KNOW, IF YOU ARE IN THE RESERVES AND YOU GO TO MONDAY NIGHT MEETINGS, EVERY THREE MONTHS THEY SEND YOU A CHECK. IT'S NOT A BIG CHECK BUT IT'S A CHECK. AND MY REACTION WHEN I GOT THE ORDERS WAS OKAY, I'VE BEEN TAKING THEIR MONEY, SO I WASN'T UPSET. YOU KNOW, I THINK EVERYBODY OUGHT TO SERVE THEIR COUNTRY. SO MY REACTION WAS, WELL, I DON'T KNOW WHAT THEY ARE GOING TO DO WITH ME, BUT OKAY, I'LL GO BACK IN, AND AT THAT TIME I WAS A SECOND CLASS PETTY OFFICER. I WAS A SECOND CLASS YEOMAN.

AND SO I LEFT EVANSVILLE AND I WENT TO LOUISVILLE AND THEN I WENT TO NORFOLK, VIRGINIA. AND WHEN I FOUND OUT WHERE I WAS GOING TO GO, I CALLED MY WIFE AND SHE MET ME IN JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA. AND I WAS ASSIGNED TO AN OUTFIT CALLED VC-62, WHICH WAS A PHOTOGRAPHY SQUADRON. THE FUNNY THING ABOUT THE NAVY, WHEN I GOT CALLED BACK IN, MY SHIP, THE USS WASP CV-18, WAS ON ACTIVE DUTY. SO I REQUESTED THAT THEY SEND ME BACK TO THE SHIP, AND THE NAVY BEING LIKE IT IS, THEY SENT ME TO A PHOTOGRAPHY SQUADRON IN JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA. AND SO I --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: NOW, WHY DID THAT DECISION COME ABOUT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: WELL, I'M NOT THE ONE THAT MAKES THE DECISIONS SO THE END RESULT WAS, I'M A SECOND CLASS YEOMAN THAT GOT ASSIGNED TO A PHOTOGRAPHY SQUADRON WHO WAS ASSIGNED TO WORK IN THE PERSONNEL OFFICE. AND, FORTUNATELY, FOR ME AFTER THAT WE HAD A FLEET WIDE EXAM AND I WENT UP FOR FIRST CLASS PETTY OFFICER, AND I TOOK THE EXAM AND I MADE FIRST CLASS, AND THEN I SERVED VC-62. OUR JOB WAS TO SEND THE DETACHMENTS OF PHOTOGRAPHY CREWS ON SHIPS. WE WERE ASSIGNED TO A SHIP, BUT WE WERE JUST TO TAKE THE PHOTOGRAPHS, AND WENT OUT -- WHEN I WENT INTO THE SQUADRON, WE HAD FAFL CATS FOR PHOTOGRAPHY WINGS, BUT ABOUT A MONTH AFTER I GOT IN THE SQUADRON THEY CHANGED IT, AND OUR PILOTS HAD TO TAKE JET TRAINING, AND THEN WE HAD LONG NOSE BANSHEE, JET BANSHEES, AND THEY HAD AN EXTRA LONG NOSE BECAUSE THAT'S WHERE THE PHOTOGRAPHY EQUIPMENT WAS PUT. SO THE PILOTS IN THE JETS, THEY DIDN'T HAVE TO TAKE THE PICTURE BY HAND. THEY TOOK THE PICTURE AUTOMATICALLY. THEY HAD NO GUNS ON THE PLANES.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: NOW, WERE THESE FOR RECONNAISSANCE PURPOSES? WHAT WERE THESE --

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: THESE WERE -- WELL, YOU ARE FIGHTING THE KOREAN WAR SO THEY'D GO OUT THERE, AND THEN THEY WOULD FLY OVER ENEMY TERRITORY AND TAKE PICTURES, AND THEN BRING IT BACK AND THEN RELAY THE PICTURES, BOTH TO THE NAVY AND THE ARMY SO THEY COULD GET THEIR TARGETS. BUT WE WOULD SEND DETACHMENTS OUT, AND THEY'D GO OUT AND THEY'D BE OUT ABOUT THREE MONTHS, AND THEY'D COME BACK IN AND THEN WE'D SEND ANOTHER DETACHMENT. I VOLUNTEERED TO GO ON A DETACHMENT BECAUSE THEY WERE GOING TO THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA BUT MY SKIPPER NEVER LET ME LEAVE.

SO MY JOB WAS TO RUN THE PERSONNEL AND ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICE IN THE SQUADRON SO I NEVER DID GET TO GO ON A DETACHMENT. SO I SPENT A YEAR-AND-A-HALF IN FLORIDA. WE WERE AT NAS JACKSON, AND THEN WE WERE ASSIGNED TO CECIL FIELD, WHICH IS ABOUT 17 MILES FROM JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA. AND I SPENT THE REST OF MY NAVY CAREER AS A FIRST CLASS. I APPLIED FOR COMMISSION BECAUSE I HAD A COLLEGE DEGREE, BUT WHEN THE COMMISSION CAME THROUGH, I TURNED IT DOWN BECAUSE MY WIFE WANTED TO GO HOME, AND IF YOU TAKE YOUR COMMISSION, YOU SERVE AT THE PLEASURE OF THE NAVY AND YOU DON'T GET TO GO HOME.

AND IF I STAYED A FIRST CLASS PETTY OFFICER, THEN MY ENLISTMENT WAS UP IN A YEAR, AND WE KNEW THAT IN MARCH OF 1952 I'D BE ABLE TO GO HOME. I WANTED TO RE-ENLIST BECAUSE I DIDN'T HAVE THAT MUCH MORE TIME TO DO, BUT MY WIFE DIDN'T LIKE THE NAVY SO WE CAME HOME.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: ANY REGRETS?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: NO. I HAVE NO REGRETS BECAUSE I SPENT 40 WONDERFUL YEARS TEACHING KIDS, BEING AN ELEMENTARY PRINCIPAL AND HAD THE BEST JOB IN THE WORLD. HOWEVER, I HAVE TO SAY I LOVE THE NAVY. I THINK IT'S WONDERFUL. I HAVE A GRANDSON THAT I TRIED TO CONVINCE TO JOIN THE NAVY. IT'S A GREAT ORGANIZATION. THE SERVICE IS A GOOD PLACE TO BE. IT IS NO DIFFERENT THAN CIVILIAN LIFE AS LONG AS YOU DO WHAT YOU ARE ASKED TO DO, YOU GET ALONG. FOR MYSELF PERSONALLY I WAS ABLE TO ADVANCE. I STARTED OUT AS A APPRENTICE SEAMAN, I ENDED UP AS A FIRST CLASS PETTY OFFICER, COULD HAVE BEEN AN OFFICER. SO THE OPPORTUNITIES TO ADVANCE IN THE SERVICE ARE THERE, AS LONG AS YOU KEEP YOUR NOSE CLEAN AND DO WHAT YOU ARE SUPPOSED TO DO. AND IT'S NO DIFFERENT THAN CIVILIAN LIFE. YOU HAVE A JOB TO DO. I PERSONALLY BELIEVE THAT EVERY YOUNG MAN SHOULD HAVE THE OPPORTUNITY TO SERVE HIS COUNTRY.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: SO MANY PEOPLE I'VE TALKED TO HAVE USED EXACTLY THAT SAME PHRASE, WE HAD A JOB TO DO. LOOKING BACK ALL THESE YEARS, HOW DO YOU ASSESS THE SCOPE AND SIZE OF THAT JOB AND WHAT YOU GUYS WERE ABLE TO ACCOMPLISH?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: OH, I HAPPENED TO BE -- AGREE WITH -- I DON'T KNOW HOW MANY PEOPLE HAS READ TOM BROKAW'S BOOK THE GREATEST GENERATION. I FEEL THAT MY GENERATION WAS BLESSED, YOU KNOW. WE HAD TO FIGHT IN WORLD WAR II, BUT I DON'T KNOW OF ANYBODY THAT HAD THE OPPORTUNITY TO SERVE THEIR COUNTRY THAT FOUGHT IN WORLD WAR II THAT REGRETS IT. ALL OF US WANTED TO GET THE JOB DONE. I THINK IT MADE A MUCH BETTER PERSON OUT OF ME PERSONALLY. IT GAVE ME OPPORTUNITIES I WOULDN'T HAVE HAD. YOU KNOW, I CAME BACK AND I'D NEVER, EVER THOUGHT ABOUT GOING TO COLLEGE.

AND THEN THE G.I. BILL CAME. AND YOU JUST THINK OF THE THOUSANDS AND THOUSANDS OF YOUNG MEN THAT WERE MY AGE THAT GOT A COLLEGE DEGREE ON THE G.I. BILL, AND THEN WERE ABLE TO GO ON WITH THEIR LIFE AND CONTRIBUTE TO THE BETTERMENT OF AMERICA. AND I PERSONALLY BELIEVE THAT -- YOU KNOW, I HAD TWO BROTHERS PLUS MYSELF. I WAS A LITTLE BIT MORE FORTUNATE THAN MY TWO BROTHERS. I HAD ONE IN THE ENGINEERS AND ONE THAT WAS A PARATROOPER, BOTH OF THEM CAME HOME ALIVE AND THAT'S WONDERFUL. BUT BOTH OF THEM GOT A PURPLE HEART, BOTH OF THEM GOT WOUNDED. I WAS BLESSED.

I DIDN'T GET WOUNDED, YOU KNOW. BUT EVEN BOTH OF MY BROTHERS ARE PROUD OF WHAT THEY DID. I THINK THERE ARE TOO MANY PEOPLE THAT REALLY DON'T KNOW THE EFFORT THAT VETERANS -- NOT JUST WORLD WAR II VETERANS BUT ANY VETERAN, WHETHER YOU ARE TALKING ABOUT KOREAN WAR, VIETNAM WAR, DESERT STORM, ANY WAR -- I'M PROUD OF THE RECORD I HAVE. I'M PROUD OF THE RECORD THAT MY FAMILY HAS. I HAD A GRANDFATHER THAT WAS A CAPTAIN IN THE SPANISH AMERICAN WAR. I HAVE AN UNCLE WHO WAS MARINE AND GOT GASSED IN WORLD WAR I.

AND THEN IN MY FAMILY I HAVE ANOTHER UNCLE THAT FOUGHT IN WORLD WAR II, PLUS I HAVE TWO BROTHERS AND MYSELF. SO SERVING YOUR COUNTRY TO ME IS ONE OF THE GREATEST HONORS YOU CAN DO. I'D GO BACK TOMORROW IF THEY NEEDED ME. BUT AS MY WIFE TELLS ME, I'M TOO OLD. YOU KNOW, WHEN YOU ARE 76, WHY -- BUT I WOULDN'T HESITATE. I WOULD HAVE LOVED TO BE ON THAT LST, THESE OLD GUYS, YOU KNOW -- AND HOPEFULLY THEY ARE GOING TO BRING IT HERE, AND I THINK PEOPLE SHOULD REALLY OUGHT TO LOOK AT THE HISTORY OF THE LST IN EVANSVILLE, INDIANA.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: I THINK IT WILL BE A HUGE TURN OUT.

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: BUT I THINK PEOPLE MY AGE DON'T REGRET THE EXPERIENCE THEY HAVE. FIRST PLACE, I COULDN'T WAIT TO GET IN THE WAR. I COULDN'T WAIT. I HAD TWO BROTHERS OVER THERE, AND I WAS WORKING ON A DAIRY FARM AND HAD THE CHANCE TO ACTUALLY STAY OUT. I COULDN'T DO THAT. I COULDN'T DO THAT. AND I WANTED TO GO IN THE NAVY AND MY NAVY EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN WONDERFUL FOR ME. THE SHIP I WAS ON, CV-18, THE MIGHTY STINGER, THE USS WASP, WE HAVE A NOT-FOR-PROFIT ORGANIZATION, AND WE MEET EVERY YEAR. WE HAVE A REUNION EVERY YEAR.

WE HAVE A ROSTER. WE HAVE A NEWSPAPER THAT'S PUT OUT QUARTERLY. WE KEEP IN TOUCH WITH EVERYBODY. LAST YEAR OUR REUNION WAS IN DULUTH. THIS YEAR WE ARE ALL GOING ON A CRUISE. NEXT YEAR MY ORGANIZATION IS GOING TO MEET IN SAN FRANCISCO. FOR OUR 50TH REUNION WE ALL MET IN BOSTON BECAUSE THAT'S WHERE OUR SHIP WAS COMMISSIONED. THEY DON'T HAVE SCULLEY SQUARE ANYMORE BUT, YOU KNOW, PLACES CHANGE. WHEN WE HAD OUR REUNION WHEN I, YOU KNOW -- WE DRY DOCKED IN BREMERTON, WHICH IS ACROSS FROM SEATTLE AND I DIDN'T RECOGNIZE SEATTLE, WASHINGTON COMPARED TO WHEN I WAS THERE IN 1946 OR '45. SO -- BUT MY ORGANIZATION, WE RAISE MONEY AND THEN PUT UP MEMORIALS TO KEEP OUR SHIP'S NAME AFLOAT.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: TELL ME WHAT IT IS THAT A CREWMEN'S LOVE FOR A SHIP, FOR THEIR SHIP, HOW DEEP IS THAT?

sp.speaker: Norbert Woolley
sp.p: TREMENDOUS. TREMENDOUS. YOU KNOW, I CALLED MY SHIP THE MIGHTY STINGER, YOU KNOW. BUT YOU TALK TO ANYBODY THAT SERVED ON MY SHIP -- I HAPPENED TO BE IN K DIVISION, BUT SOME OF MY BEST FRIENDS OFF OF MY SHIP TODAY WERE IN E DIVISION. THEY WERE ELECTRICIANS, BUT WE GOT TO KNOW EACH OTHER AT THE REUNIONS, BUT THERE IS A CAMARADERIE WHEN YOU SERVE ON A SHIP THAT NEVER GOES AWAY, NEVER, AND YOU THINK OF THAT SHIP AND YOU THINK OF THE PEOPLE THAT SERVED ON IT, THEY'RE SPECIAL. THEY ARE SPECIAL PEOPLE, AND YOU DON'T FORGET THAT. YOU KNOW, EVEN THOUGH THEY MAY NOT HAVE BEEN IN MY DIVISION, THERE'S A CAMARADERIE THAT IS DEVELOPED, I DON'T CARE WHAT SHIP YOU ARE ON.

IN MY CASE IN MY SHIPMATE'S CASE, IT'S THE USS WASP WITH MY EXPERIENCE. SAME IS TRUE WITH OTHERS. THERE'S A BOND. YOU KNOW, WHEN MY SHIP GOT HIT, EVERYBODY PULLED TOGETHER. TAKE THE GUYS THAT DIDN'T GO TO SICK BAY, WHY DIDN'T THEY GO TO SICK BAY BECAUSE THEY KNEW OTHER PEOPLE NEEDED THE HELP MORE. YOU DON'T THINK ABOUT YOURSELF. YOU THINK ABOUT THE SHIP, AND YOU THINK ABOUT HELPING YOUR FELLOW SHIPMATE. YOU DON'T -- YOU KNOW, IF YOU LOOK AT THE FLAG OF IWO JIMA, HOW MANY GUYS GOT KILLED TRYING TO RAISE THAT FLAG. YOU DON'T THINK ABOUT THAT. NOW, ARE YOU SCARED? SURE, YOU ARE SCARED. YOU SEE PEOPLE, YOU ARE BOUND TO GET SCARED.

PEOPLE HAVE ASKED ME -- I'VE HAD STUDENTS ASK ME WERE YOU SCARED, MR. WOOLLEY? YES, I'M SCARED. BUT THAT DOESN'T ENTER YOUR MIND WHEN YOUR SHIP GETS HIT OR WHEN YOU ARE IN A SITUATION WHERE YOU REALLY NEED TO HELP PEOPLE. WHAT YOU THINK ABOUT IS SAVING THE SHIP, SAVING YOUR BUDDY, AND YOU NEVER LOSE THAT CAMARADERIE, NEVER. I LOOK FORWARD TO EVERY YEAR TO GO TO MY REUNION, PLUS WE'VE GOT A ROSTER -- PLUS I PICK UP THE PHONE, AND I CALL PROBABLY 15 GUYS FOUR OR FIVE TIMES A YEAR JUST TO SEE HOW THEY ARE. I WAS ON MY WAY TO GO TO FLORIDA ON VACATION AND I STOPPED AND MET A BUDDY OF MINE THAT WAS AN ELECTRICIAN.

HE'S 81, FLIES HIS OWN PLANE. AND MY WIFE AND I WENT TO BAXLEY, GEORGIA AND SPENT A COUPLE DAYS WITH MALCOLM AND WINFRED. YOU JUST BUILD THAT TOGETHERNESS. AND I DON'T SEE THAT BUILT TODAY. I HATE TO SAY THAT BUT I DON'T. THAT'S WHY I THINK THAT LOOKING BACK, I HAVE NO REGRETS. I THINK IT'S ONE OF THE GREATEST EXPERIENCES I EVER HAD IN MY LIFE. I WOULD TAKE NOTHING FOR IT. AND I'D LIKE TO SEE MORE YOUNG PEOPLE GET THAT TYPE OF SPIRIT FROM THE UNITED STATES. WE LIVE IN THE GREATEST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD, AND I APPRECIATE THIS OPPORTUNITY TO PUT ON TAPE THE EXPERIENCE THAT I'VE HAD ON MY SHIP, THE USS WASP, IN WORLD WAR II. AND I WANT TO THANK LARRY AND I WANT TO THANK SENATOR LUGAR.
(CONCLUSION OF INTERVIEW.)
